details:
**Dr. Pangloss and "the best of all possible worlds"**
Pangloss is Candide's tutor, and Voltaire uses him to mock the optimism of the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz. He teaches "metaphysico-theologo-cosmolonigology" and keeps saying that "all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds," however much he suffers. He catches syphilis from the maid Paquette, is hanged at an auto-da-fé, and still turns up alive later as a galley slave near Constantinople.

**Cunegonde**
Cunegonde is the daughter of Baron Thunder-ten-Tronckh and the woman Candide loves. She is owned jointly by the Jew Don Issachar and the Grand Inquisitor, and later becomes the mistress of the governor of Buenos Aires. By the end she has become ugly, but Candide marries her anyway.

**Castle Thunder-ten-Tronckh in Westphalia**
The novel opens at this baron's castle in Westphalia, where Candide grows up alongside Cunegonde. He is kicked out after the Baron catches him kissing Cunegonde behind a screen, which starts his travels around the world. Before that, Cunegonde watched Pangloss give "experimental physics" lessons to the chambermaid Paquette in the bushes.

**El Dorado**
El Dorado is a hidden utopia in South America where gold and jewels lie on the ground like pebbles. Its people never pray to God for anything because they have nothing to ask for; they only thank him. Candide rides in a carriage pulled by sheep to meet the king. Candide and Cacambo leave with enormous wealth, and most of it is soon lost.

**"We must cultivate our garden" (Il faut cultiver notre jardin)**
This is the novel's famous last line. Candide says it to Pangloss after he has given up Pangloss's optimism. He and his companions settle on a small farm near Constantinople and decide that steady work, not philosophizing, is what keeps away boredom, vice and poverty.

**Cacambo**
Cacambo is Candide's loyal, resourceful valet, of part-Spanish descent. He travels with Candide to El Dorado and later goes to Buenos Aires to buy back Cunegonde. He also talks the cannibal Oreillons out of eating Candide by proving Candide is not a Jesuit.

**The Old Woman (daughter of Pope Urban X)**
The Old Woman is Cunegonde's servant. She was once the Princess of Palestrina and is the illegitimate daughter of the made-up Pope Urban X. She later became a slave in Morocco, and one of her buttocks was cut off to feed starving soldiers during a siege, so she has only one left. She claims nobody has had a more miserable life than hers. In a note, Voltaire praised his own discretion for inventing a pope rather than naming a real one.

**The 1755 Lisbon earthquake and the auto-da-fé**
Candide and Pangloss arrive in Lisbon just as the real 1755 earthquake strikes. The authorities then hold an auto-da-fé, a public ritual punishing supposed heretics, to prevent more earthquakes: Candide is flogged and Pangloss is hanged. Voltaire uses the disaster to attack the idea that all suffering is for the best.

**Red sheep**
Candide and Cacambo leave El Dorado with about 100 large red sheep loaded with gold and jewels. Almost all of them die on the journey. The Dutch pirate Mynheer Vanderdendur steals two of the last ones, and Candide later recovers only one of them from a sunken ship.

**Jacques the Anabaptist**
Jacques is a kind Dutch Anabaptist who takes Candide in when everyone else refuses to help him. He drowns when their ship sinks near Lisbon. Pangloss stops Candide from trying to save him, arguing that the Bay of Lisbon was made specifically so that Jacques could drown in it.

**Don Issachar and the Grand Inquisitor**
These two men share Cunegonde as their mistress in Lisbon. Candide kills Don Issachar with a sword when Issachar finds them together, and then kills the Grand Inquisitor as well. He then has to run off to South America.

**The two monkeys and the Oreillons**
In South America, Candide shoots two monkeys he sees chasing two women, and then learns the women were the monkeys' lovers. Soon afterward the Oreillons, a cannibal tribe, nearly cook him because they think he is a Jesuit.

**Martin the Manichaean**
Martin is a pessimistic scholar whom Candide picks in Suriname to travel with him to Europe. Candide chose him by holding a contest for the unhappiest man. Martin follows Manichaeism, a belief that evil rules the world, and tells Candide that "all is evil," which makes him Pangloss's opposite. He is often said to be based on the skeptic philosopher Pierre Bayle.

**The Bulgarian army and the 72,000 lashes**
After being expelled from the castle, Candide is tricked into joining the Bulgarian army, Voltaire's satire of Frederick the Great's Prussia. When he goes for a walk he is arrested as a deserter, and he chooses to run a gauntlet of 2,000 soldiers 36 times (72,000 blows) rather than take 12 bullets in the head. After two runs he begs to be shot instead, but the king pardons him.

**Admiral Byng's execution, "to encourage the others"**
On the way to Venice, Candide watches an English admiral being shot. This is based on the real 1757 execution of Admiral John Byng. Candide is told the English kill an admiral now and then "to encourage the others" (pour encourager les autres), and he refuses to set foot in England. In Venice, Candide later dines with six deposed kings and visits the bored art collector Count Pococurante.
